Seasonal indeterminacy: the physical sun altitude swings 83%

The refraction fix is more fragile than the coordinate contamination above already shows. By declaring the sun's apparent 5,733 km altitude an "optical illusion" caused by n(r), the dome commits the physical sun to an altitude bounded above by H(r) at the sun's current orbital radius. But the dome's sun is not stationary on the disc: it traces a seasonal circuit between the Tropic of Cancer at the June solstice (dome radius r ≈ 7,400 km) and the Tropic of Capricorn at the December solstice (r ≈ 12,600 km), crossing the equator (r ≈ 10,008 km) at each equinox. The ceiling H(r) = 8,537 × exp(−r/8,619) km is monotonic, so the sun's physical-altitude cap is a different number every season.

Evaluating the dome's own H(r) at the solstice and equinox radii:

  • June solstice (Tropic of Cancer, r = 7,400 km): H = 8,537 × exp(−0.858) ≈ 3,618 km. The physical sun must sit below ~3,618 km.
  • Equinoxes (equator, r = 10,008 km): H = 8,537 × exp(−1.161) ≈ 2,672 km.
  • December solstice (Tropic of Capricorn, r = 12,600 km): H = 8,537 × exp(−1.462) ≈ 1,978 km. The physical sun must sit below ~1,975 km.

The dome's refraction fix therefore commits the physical sun to a seasonally indeterminate altitude in the range 1,975 km (December) to 3,618 km (June) — an 83% swing relative to the lower bound — while the apparent altitude is held suspiciously fixed at 5,733 km year-round. The numbers above are computed directly from the dome's own functional form using the dome's own parameters: nothing here is contested arithmetic. What is contested is whether the model can absorb the consequence.

The cascade is a two-step squeeze on n(r). First, to preserve a constant apparent altitude through a varying physical altitude, the medium would have to perform exactly the right amount of extra refractive lift at each season — bending sunlight from a physical 1,978 km up to an apparent 5,733 km in December (a 3,755 km lift) and from a physical 3,618 km up to the same apparent 5,733 km in June (a 2,115 km lift). The medium's refraction must therefore be 78% stronger in December than in June. But n(r) is a function of one variable — the radial coordinate on the disc — with no time dependence whatever. The same medium cannot produce two different refractive lifts at the same radial position depending on calendar date. Second, if the physical sun is instead held at the minimum-of-cap (1,975 km) year-round to avoid the December violation, the same n(r) must take 1,975 km up to 5,733 km in every season — a factor-of-three refractive lift that would simultaneously have to leave Gaia's 10-microarcsecond stellar positions undisturbed across 1.8 billion catalogued stars. The same medium cannot do both, and the dome's n(r) has no degrees of freedom left to try.

This cascade carries beyond the coordinate system into the tidal, structural, and astrometric WINs. Tidal predictions that anchor on a fixed subsolar-point altitude (see WIN-046, semidiurnal solar S2) inherit the seasonal indeterminacy: a sun whose physical altitude halves between June and December produces a tidal forcing function that is itself seasonally varying, yet the observed S2 amplitude and phase hold constant across seasons to fractional-percent precision. Solar-elevation-from-H(r) predictions (WIN-056) face the constraint from the other direction: the very H(r) function that supplies a fixed-looking ceiling collapses into a seasonally swinging one when the sun is allowed to move. And every WIN downstream of H(r) or the coordinate system — the firmament scaling function (WIN-044), Schumann cavity geometry (WIN-002, WIN-029) — inherits the contradiction at one remove.

anticipated_objections.objection: Seasonal variation in physical sun altitude is unproblematic in itself — Earth has seasons too, with declination varying through the year by ±23.4°. A dome model accommodating a seasonally varying sun altitude is no more ad hoc than a globe model accommodating axial tilt.
anticipated_objections.response: The globe's seasonal variation is a deductive consequence of two prior commitments — axial tilt and spherical geometry — and is parameter-free at the seasonal-amplitude level. The dome's published model lists sun altitude as a single value (5,733 km apparent, posited <4,200 km physical). The model contains no seasonal-amplitude curve, no axial-tilt analogue, no published functional form for physical sun altitude vs date. Adding one is a free parameter — and one that must be calibrated to make the apparent altitude come out constant through n(r), which is itself calibrated to make Polaris observations come out correct, which is itself a free fit. Each layer of fix adds parameters without adding predictive content, which is the failure mode the refraction fix was supposed to escape.

anticipated_objections.objection: The physical sun could simply sit at the minimum-of-cap altitude (1,975 km) year-round, with the apparent altitude (5,733 km) produced by n(r) doing the same 3,758 km of refractive lift in every season. This is internally consistent.
anticipated_objections.response: This is the cleanest defense and the EXP addresses it explicitly: holding the physical sun at 1,975 km year-round preserves consistency with H(r) at every radius the sun crosses (since H(r) ≥ 1,978 km for all r ≤ 12,600 km). But it then commits n(r) to lifting the apparent sun from 1,975 km up to 5,733 km — a factor-of-three lift requiring refractive indices that, applied to stellar light, would displace Gaia's catalogued positions by amounts many orders of magnitude above the measured 10-microarcsecond precision. The dome cannot have it both ways: the same n(r) must refract sunlight strongly enough to lift 1,975 km to 5,733 km, yet refract starlight weakly enough to leave Gaia astrometry intact. n(r) has no wavelength dependence in the published formula, so there is no escape via 'optical n is high but radio n is low.' This is the closure that makes Section 1.8 land.

anticipated_objections.objection: The 83% figure is a rhetorical inflation — the absolute swing is 1,640 km, which sounds smaller than 83%.
anticipated_objections.response: Both framings are accurate. 1,640 km absolute swing is the geometric fact; 83% relative to the lower bound is the percent of the lower bound that the upper bound exceeds. The 83% framing is the standard way of expressing a seasonal swing in atmospheric and oceanographic literature (e.g., 'sea-ice extent swings 83% between winter and summer maxima') and is not pejorative. The text gives both the absolute numbers (1,975 and 3,618 km) and the percent, so the reader can choose the framing that lands.

anticipated_objections.objection: Sun-altitude-from-H(r) (WIN-056) is the original anchor of the 5,733 km conflict — citing it as a downstream casualty is double-counting.
anticipated_objections.response: The cross-reference to WIN-056 here is for a different reason: WIN-056 derives the apparent solar altitude FROM H(r) and finds it conflicts with the observed 5,733 km. This EXP makes the corollary explicit — the same H(r) function that produces the conflict ALSO yields a seasonally swinging ceiling when the sun is allowed to move. WIN-056's framing is 'H(r) gives the wrong altitude'; this section's framing is 'H(r) gives a different wrong altitude in every season.' Both are valid, mutually-reinforcing critiques, not duplicates.

kernel_of_truth: The dome's H(r) = 8,537 × exp(−r/8,619) is a smooth, monotonic, well-conditioned mathematical function. Given fixed parameters, it yields determinate values everywhere — there is nothing computationally pathological about the function itself. The seasonal-indeterminacy critique does NOT claim that H(r) is mathematically broken; it claims that H(r), once interpreted physically AND combined with a sun that traces a real seasonal circuit, generates an internal-consistency obligation the dome has not yet discharged. Recognising the mathematical determinacy of H(r) sharpens rather than weakens the critique: the inconsistency is structural, not computational.
why_kernel_doesnt_save_claim: A mathematically determinate H(r) is only useful for prediction if the physical objects it constrains are themselves consistently parameterised. The dome's sun moves seasonally (by uncontested observation); H(r) takes different values along that motion; the refraction fix bounds the physical sun by H(r) at each radius. These three commitments together force a seasonally varying physical sun altitude — which then forces n(r) into a time-dependent or factor-of-three role n(r) cannot fill. The H(r) function is fine. The combination of H(r) + refraction fix + observed seasonal sun motion is not.
